title: East Bay Upscale Indian Dining Wave Gains Momentum
excerpt: Pippal's Dublin opening anchors a new generation of elevated Indian restaurants — with regional tasting menus, craft cocktails, and Karnataka home cooking. According to Diablo Magazine, the East Bay is finally catching up.
body:
• Pippal, a regional-Indian restaurant from the Rivaaz Hospitality Group, opened in Dublin's Waterford Place shopping center last fall — the highest-profile arrival in a wave of upscale modern Indian dining sweeping the East Bay, according to Diablo Magazine.
  • The newcomers span the Tri-Valley and beyond: Sanjeev Kapoor's Yellow Chilli in Danville, Khaki Bar and Indian Canteen in San Ramon's Bishop Ranch, Essence Redefining Indian Food in Livermore, and Bangalore Blues in Berkeley.
  • Worth a visit: Pippal's chef Munish Rana cooks a new tasting menu each month built around a different Indian region — tribal dishes from Chhattisgarh and Jharkhand one month, Sikkim-chilli chaat and Himalayan momos the next. In Berkeley, Bangalore Blues serves Karnataka specialties like ghee-roasted dosas and curries that take up to seven hours to prepare.
  • Bar programs are going Indian too: Pippal's Kerala Backwaters spikes vodka with South Indian rasam, while the Yellow Chilli pours a jaljeera vodkatini.

The East Bay's Indian food scene is in the middle of a transformation. Pippal, a sleek regional-Indian restaurant from the Rivaaz Hospitality Group that opened in Dublin's Waterford Place last fall, is the highest-profile example of an ambitious wave of upscale restaurants redefining Indian food east of the Bay, Diablo Magazine reports.

Context & Background

For years, the East Bay trailed San Francisco and the South Bay when it came to elevated Indian dining. The local scene was dominated by smaller, budget-conscious eateries serving the heartier, curry-heavy dishes of northern India. According to Diablo, that is changing fast, driven by a new generation of restaurateurs shifting perceptions of the cuisine.

Leading the charge is Anu Bhambri, who cofounded the Rivaaz Hospitality Group with her partner Taresh Anand after moving from Delhi to the Bay Area for a tech career. Rivaaz operates several elevated Indian concepts — including the original Pippal in Emeryville and the modern Indian concept Rooh — with Bollywood actor and model Jatin Grewal and his wife Carolina taking a lead role in launching the Dublin location.

The shift reached the East Bay suburbs four years ago with the debut of the Yellow Chilli — celebrity chef Sanjeev Kapoor's flagship franchise — in Danville's Rose Garden shopping center. Co-owner Shivraj Sidhu says it offered an experience "you don't see [with] any other Indian restaurants around here." He followed it with Essence Redefining Indian Food, an expansive Livermore concept that has drawn similar crowds across the Tri-Valley and Central Valley.

Impact & Analysis

The new menus reach far beyond the chicken tikka masala, samosas, and garlic naan standards. Khaki Bar and Indian Canteen, which opened last year in San Ramon's City Center Bishop Ranch with the Sarkar brothers, still serves butter chicken — founder Akash Kapoor admits "you have to put butter chicken on the menu" — but also plates Delhi street-style kebabs, fried jackfruit and potato cutlets from Kolkata, and a whole butterflied branzino in banana leaf with Kerala coconut-tomato masala.

At Pippal, the regional focus is the entire concept. Executive chef Munish Rana creates a new tasting menu every month inspired by a different part of India: Goa and Maharashtra in May, tribal flavors from Chhattisgarh and Jharkhand in June, and the mountainous Northeast in July — with chaat flavored with Sikkim's dalle chilies, handmade momos in roasted tomato jhol, and Himalayan ghathuk noodle soup.

"It's not just chicken tikka masala, it's not biryani, and it's not samosa: It's 10,000 other things and 50 other cuisines."

— Akash Kapoor, Founder, Curry Up Now and Khaki Bar and Indian Canteen

Bar programs are following suit: cardamom bitters and jaggery in Khaki's AK Old Fashioned, rasam in Pippal's Kerala Backwaters, and mango chutney in the Mahal Mule at Taj Mahal Flavors of India.

Diaspora Angle

For the East Bay's Indian diaspora, the new wave delivers something the old scene rarely offered: flavors from India's less-celebrated regions, cooked with a seriousness that echoes home. In Berkeley, entrepreneur Aravind Pochiraju opened Bangalore Blues to reproduce the scratch-made methods of his Karnataka childhood — grinding imported whole spices by hand, roasting dosas in house-made ghee, and slow-cooking layered South Indian curries for up to seven hours.

"It doesn't have to all be cheap lunch buffets. There's always a place for that, but there's also a place for a more upscale dining experience."

— Anu Bhambri, Cofounder, Rivaaz Hospitality Group

What's Next

The momentum shows no sign of slowing. Dublin's dining corridor keeps filling in — Pippal landed at 4500 Tassajara Road in December 2025, part of a twelve-month burst that also brought H Mart's first East Bay grocery, Mendocino Farms, and Marufuku Ramen, per local commercial coverage. As the East Bay stops being the afterthought on the Bay Area's Indian dining map, the question is no longer whether upscale Indian dining belongs here — it's which region's flavors to try first.
